extracted.intended_audience: general readers, film students, screenwriters, critics and filmmakers interested in the romantic comedy film genre
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and analyze the conventions, themes, character types, historical influences, and variations that define romantic comedy films (romcoms), and how contemporary works may adapt or subvert those conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core definition / focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Romantic comedy (commonly shortened to romcom or rom‑com) is a sub-genre of comedy and romance fiction, focusing on lighthearted, humorous plot lines centered on romantic ideas, such as how love is able to surmount all obstacles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the defining criterion: plot centered on romance with comedic tone; examples include classic Hollywood romcoms. Works should prioritize romantic relationship and humor as central elements rather than treating one as merely incidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and typical resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: A romantic comedy is 'a light‑hearted and happily concluded manner which usually avoids serious satire' (Oxford Dictionary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect light tone and a generally happy or hopeful ending; avoidance of sustained, serious satire distinguishes romcoms from darker comedies or tragicomedies. Note: contemporary examples may subvert this, but the traditional expectation is a satisfying romantic resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on follies and misunderstandings of lovers
rubrics_metrics.description: Romantic comedies 'deal mainly with the follies and misunderstandings of young lovers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central conflicts often arise from miscommunication, misunderstandings, or character flaws rather than external catastrophe. Evaluations should look for how these interpersonal issues drive comedy and ultimately lead to reconciliation or growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet‑cute / contrived romantic encounter
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the conventions is the 'meet‑cute', a humorous or unexpected encounter that creates initial tension and sets up the romantic storyline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common devices: awkwardness, clash of personalities or beliefs, embarrassing situations, comical misunderstandings, or mistaken identity. Examples: repeated accidental meetings (Lost and Found), scripted awkward first encounters. A strong meet‑cute establishes chemistry and stakes quickly; anti-pattern: a flat, exposition-heavy first meeting that fails to generate comedic tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character role reversals / screwball dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Screwball comedies and some romcoms 'use reversal of gender roles to add comedic effect' and contain characters who diverge from socially imposed gender roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for sharp, rapid dialogue, battle-of-the-sexes plotting, role reversal (e.g., emotionally open male leads, domineering female leads), and farcical situations. This is a stylistic and character-driven sub-criterion distinguishing screwball‑influenced romcoms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgenre variants (career woman, sex comedy, bromantic, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Romantic comedy developed into sub-genres like screwball comedies, career woman comedies, and 1950s sex comedies; related forms include bromantic comedy, chick flick, and romantic comedy television series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works against the expectations of these subgenres: e.g., career woman comedies foreground workplace and gender dynamics; sex comedies foreground sexual themes and adult situations. The presence of subgenre markers shifts tone, themes, and acceptable comedic devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of unusual premises or genre blending for originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Some romantic comedies adopt special circumstances (e.g., Warm Bodies where a zombie falls in love with a human; Zack and Miri Make a Porno where protagonists make a pornographic film) to add originality while maintaining romcom structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality can come from blending romcom structure with fantasy, horror, or meta premises; assessment should consider whether the unusual premise serves the romantic and comedic core or distracts from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to subvert the traditional happy ending
rubrics_metrics.description: Some romantic comedies flip conventions so protagonists do not end up together or end separated but content (e.g., 500 Days of Summer, Adam).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern evaluations should allow for nontraditional outcomes as deliberate artistic choices. Assess whether subversion still honors romcom elements (romantic focus, humor, growth) or abandons the genre's core identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic expansion to more complex/adult topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary romcoms sometimes explore more complex topics such as marriage, responsibility, disability, and mental illness (examples: This Is 40, Knocked Up, Silver Linings Playbook).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how well serious themes are integrated without losing the comedic-romantic core. Success is measured by credible character development and tonal balance between humor and substantive issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation and perspective diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically the genre 'has centered the perspectives of the "rich, white, thin and straight"', but streaming services have increased variety of characters and viewpoints by taking more chances on underrepresented perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate inclusiveness of protagonists, settings, and cultural viewpoints. Greater diversity can refresh conventions; anti-pattern: tokenism or reinforcing narrow stereotypes while claiming diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and literary influences shaping conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Romantic comedy evolved from Ancient Greek comedy, medieval romance, and 18th‑century Restoration comedy, influencing its emphasis on social rules, marriage plots, and the follies of lovers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding these historical influences helps evaluate structural elements (e.g., marriage-market plots, comedy of manners) and whether a modern work consciously engages with or updates those traditions.
